articles.title: Five touchdowns for BeckhmJr. Three punts for Dorrill.
articles.dek: Mossdeep beat Petalburg 55–0 behind seven Dram Marino touchdown passes, yet the Eclipse coach had several possessions he wanted explained.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Michael Dorrill had three punts to discuss after a 55–0 victory. Each of those Mossdeep possessions gained seven yards. Each ended with Adam Vinathorn sending the ball away. Accel BeckhmJr could reasonably expect five touchdown catches to command most of the conversation, but his coach had located twenty-one unproductive yards and was prepared to give them considerable attention.

“We had the ball eleven times and punted three times,” Dorrill said. “Which of those possessions are you telling me didn't count? We don't get to decide that because the other team hasn't scored. Somebody explain the first down, explain the protection, explain why we needed the punt team.”

There was plenty to praise before that review began. Dram Marino completed nineteen of twenty-four passes for 298 yards and seven touchdowns without an interception. BeckhmJr caught all nine of his targets for 172 yards and five scores. Shawn Mareman rushed for 103 yards and a touchdown, then added a receiving touchdown. The Eclipse improved to 13–0, while a Petalburg club that arrived with nine victories left having failed to score in any quarter.

The result also supplied a forceful answer to anyone expecting Mossdeep's injury absences to produce an immediate offensive retreat. Ninjaskamara remained unavailable. Mareman handled seventeen carries, Poury Holt contributed twenty-five yards on five attempts, and Marino found four different receivers for gains beyond the basic work of BeckhmJr. Mossdeep finished with 443 total yards and converted six of nine third downs. The Pride managed one conversion in twelve attempts.
Five catches that ended possessions

body.alt: Editorial illustration of Dram Marino (Drampa), number 12.
body.caption: Dram Marino threw seven touchdown passes against Petalburg.

body.text: BeckhmJr's first touchdown arrived at 3:50 of the opening quarter, on a thirty-six-yard pass deep right. Mareman had opened the three-play possession with a sixteen-yard run up the middle, and Marino had followed with a twelve-yard completion to BeckhmJr. The three snaps covered sixty-four yards. Petalburg's first punt had barely faded from relevance before Mossdeep had taken the lead.

The Eclipse then produced the first of the possessions that irritated Dorrill. Kabutops sacked Marino for six yards on first down, and the drive ended after gaining seven. Petalburg could take encouragement from the stop and from a second Kabutops sack early in the next quarter. The problem was what happened around those moments: the Pride could stop a possession, but they couldn't put together an answer of their own.

Mossdeep's next touchdown came at the end of a nine-play, fifty-two-yard drive. Marino found Mareman short right for twelve yards at 4:42 of the second quarter. That scoring pass established a pattern Petalburg never solved. The Eclipse could finish through a receiver, a tight end or a running back, and the defense still had to account for the next deep throw to BeckhmJr.

That throw arrived on the following Mossdeep possession. Marino hit BeckhmJr deep right for forty-eight yards at 3:26, completing a two-play, fifty-nine-yard touchdown drive. The receiver had already scored twice from the same broad side of the field at different distances. Calling for another defender to pay attention to him would have been a reasonable opening point in Petalburg's discussion; actually limiting the entire offense required considerably more.

“I caught the ones he sent me,” BeckhmJr said. “Apparently that's a good way to get him to send another. I'm willing to keep testing it.” The receiver's mischievous satisfaction had numerical support. Nine targets produced nine catches, and more than half those receptions ended in the end zone. Marino's careful explanation was shorter: “The completion has to be there. Once it is, get it to him and let him finish.”

BeckhmJr added a thirty-yard touchdown deep left with 2:07 remaining in the third quarter, an eleven-yard score short right with three seconds left in that period, and a two-yard touchdown short right with thirty-nine seconds left in the game. The five scores covered different parts of the field and different stages of possessions. Petalburg had to defend the full route before it could worry about the receiver's running after the catch.
Seven sacks and three interceptions

body.alt: Editorial illustration of Joey Sporeter (Breloom), number 98.
body.caption: Joey Sporeter recorded 3.5 of Mossdeep’s seven sacks.

body.text: Joey Sporeter sacked Iron Valiant on Petalburg's first offensive snap. Derrat Brooks added another sack later in that opening possession, and the Pride eventually punted. That beginning mattered because Petalburg spent much of the afternoon trying to repair long-yardage situations rather than choosing freely from its offense. Oinkologne's ten carries produced seventeen yards. Iron Valiant finished fourteen of thirty for 137 yards, three interceptions and seven sacks taken.

Sporeter received credit for three and a half sacks and ten pressures. Ray Glewis, Brooks and Will Shells each received a sack, while Armaldo Pace had a half-sack. The play log records Sporeter repeatedly reaching the quarterback, including a fourth-quarter sack immediately before Clay Rathews intercepted a third-and-sixteen throw. Individual rushing success and coverage success kept appearing in the same possessions.

“You get another chance every time they line up,” Sporeter said. “I try to make the next one useful. You can enjoy the sack after the ball's dead.” His relaxed delivery suited a defense that had ample reason to feel secure without giving Petalburg an easy final possession.

Electric Berry supplied Mossdeep's first interception at 3:09 of the second quarter, taking a third-and-ten throw deep left and returning it seventeen yards. Marino completed the ensuing twenty-nine-yard touchdown drive with a four-yard pass short left to Gronkaludon. DeFro Buckner intercepted another deep throw at 1:23, returning it twenty yards. Mareman finished the next drive with a one-yard run to the right.

Those two interceptions helped Mossdeep score twenty-seven points in the second quarter and lead 34–0 at halftime. Petalburg's offense had produced neither the field position nor the points needed to restrain the game's pace. The Pride's seven punts and three interceptions provided repeated opportunities for an opponent already converting ordinary possessions into touchdowns.

The defense retained its concentration through the closing seconds. Iron Valiant completed a twenty-two-yard pass to Golbat on Petalburg's last drive, but Sporeter sacked him on the next snap. Shells added another sack later in the possession. At one second remaining, Parasect ran right on fourth-and-four and gained nothing, with Rathews making the tackle. The shutout survived the final play.
The corrections travel to Canalave

Mossdeep's other offensive contributors made the headline numbers easier to produce. Gronkaludon caught six passes for sixty-one yards and a touchdown. Ninjulio Jones had forty-six receiving yards and fourteen more on a rushing attempt. Lorenzo Steel caught a seven-yard pass. Mareman's combination of running and receiving gave the Eclipse a productive answer when the ball stayed underneath.

The record also contains two sacks allowed, three punts and a missed extra point. Those details will occupy more of Dorrill's review than the final margin would suggest. Each punt followed a possession that gained seven yards, a repeated outcome he can examine separately without treating every stalled series as the same mistake. “I'm pleased they kept them out of the end zone,” he said. “I'm pleased we finished eight drives. Then we go through everything that didn't meet the standard. You can rest when you've won the championship. We haven't done that.”

Petalburg falls to 9–4 and visits Pastoria next. The Pride still have a substantial season to protect, but this game exposed how little room they had once the rushing attack stalled. A defense that forced three punts needed some offensive relief; a quarterback facing repeated long-yardage snaps needed the running game to create better ones. Both problems now demand attention before another road trip.

Mossdeep travels to 7–6 Canalave, which has just been shut out 17–0 by Sunyshore. The Eclipse's injury list still includes Ninjaskamara for two weeks, Richard Furman for three, and Marshall Flock and Luvrelle Revis for one each. Gronkaludon's new minor entry reports no remaining absence. Those are the available reports, not guarantees about future workloads. BeckhmJr's five touchdown catches are already recorded; Dorrill's next meeting can begin with the three possessions that ended in punts.

art.alt: Editorial illustration of Accel BeckhmJr (Accelgor), number 11.

articles.title: Jolt Train Ln takes the long way home, twice
articles.dek: Two punt-return touchdowns and five Archam Manning scoring passes turn a 14–3 halftime lead into a 56–6 win before Saffron visits Mt. Silver.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Jolt Train Ln gave Saffron sixty-five yards on one punt return and seventy-seven on another. Both ended in touchdowns. Viridian's offense spent the afternoon trying to assemble gains in smaller pieces, then watched the Psi Corps cover the field while its own punt unit was supposed to be ending a possession. By the time Saffron finished a 56–6 victory, the returner had also intercepted a pass.

Trent Scarboro wanted the other members of those units included in the conversation. “Everybody sees him finish,” the Saffron coach said. “I love that. I want everybody seeing the guys who give him a chance, too. You commit to that job, you believe the next return can change the game, and then you get something like this. Those are our guys doing it together.”

The victory moves Saffron to 11–2 before a visit to 12–1 Mt. Silver. It is a far more imposing result than the 14–3 halftime score suggested. The Psi Corps scored twenty-one points in each of the final two quarters, produced five touchdown passes from Archam Manning, and rushed for 216 yards. Viridian got two field goals from Octillery and no touchdowns from an offense that accumulated 304 yards.

That distinction between gaining territory and finishing possessions was central to the game. The Titans ran sixty-six offensive plays to Saffron's forty-six and earned fifteen first downs. They still punted six times, threw two interceptions and lost a fumble. Saffron supplied enough scoring outside its ordinary offense that Viridian's longer stretches with the ball never gave the game the shape the Titans needed.
The return that changed the third quarter

body.alt: Editorial illustration of Dam Skattebo (Darmanitan), number 22.
body.caption: Dam Skattebo gained 155 rushing yards against Viridian.

body.text: Viridian's first possession after halftime ended with a punt from Octillery at 5:28 of the third quarter. Jolt Train Ln took it at the Saffron thirty-five and returned it sixty-five yards for a touchdown. The score extended an eleven-point halftime advantage and immediately made the Titans' next offensive possession more urgent.

That possession lasted one play. Ampharos intercepted Mr. Rime's short throw left and returned it fourteen yards. Saffron then needed only two offensive snaps to score again, with Manning finding Bysson Witten short right for a two-yard touchdown at 4:39. Two touchdowns had arrived through a return and a brief offensive possession before Viridian could restore any rhythm.

The sequence illustrates why a special-teams score can change more than the margin. Saffron's offense did not have to consume a long drive to make the first touchdown. Its defense returned immediately and produced the interception that shortened the second. The Titans' next possession lasted seven plays and gained twenty-eight yards, but it ended in another punt. By then Saffron had made every ordinary exchange considerably more expensive.

Scarboro's response to the sequence was characteristically personal. “I want them to feel what happens when they keep showing up for one another,” he said. “You get a return, the defense comes out and gets the ball, the offense finishes. That's a whole sideline seeing the work pay off. Now you've got to bring that same effort to the next possession.”

Saffron did. Its next scoring drive covered eighty yards in eight plays, ending when Manning threw short right to Dam Skattebo for a four-yard touchdown with seventeen seconds left in the third. The Psi Corps had opened the half through special teams and defense, then finished the quarter with a sustained offensive drive. Viridian had to deal with all three routes to the scoreboard.
Skattebo supplies the running game

Skattebo rushed fourteen times for 155 yards and a touchdown, with a longest gain of forty-three. Emmitt Smoth added forty-nine yards on five carries, and Gengar Pickens contributed twelve on three. Saffron's running backs repeatedly gained enough to keep Manning from carrying the entire offense. The team needed only four third-down attempts and converted two.

“We had room, and I tried to use it properly,” Skattebo said. “The people helping me get through there deserve some of that attention. It's a good day when you can make their work count.” His account was gentle; the impact of his rushing was not. Fourteen attempts at an average of 11.1 yards gave Saffron an efficient way to move through possessions even when the passing game made mistakes.

Manning threw two interceptions. Sigilyph took a short pass right on the opening drive, and Sneasel intercepted a deep throw right early in the fourth quarter. Each gave Viridian an opportunity, and each resulted in a field goal rather than a touchdown. The Titans briefly led 3–0 after Octillery's fifty-five-yard kick in the first quarter. Their next score, a thirty-two-yard field goal, did not arrive until the fourth.

Between those kicks, Saffron had answered the opening interception with an eighty-three-yard touchdown drive. Manning hit HeeDee Lamb deep right for twenty-one yards at the end of it. Skattebo finished the following sixty-five-yard drive with a four-yard run up the middle. The Psi Corps led 14–3 at halftime even after a later possession ended on downs.

The offense therefore had a clear source of dissatisfaction alongside the production. It gave away two possessions through interceptions and another through a failed fourth-down series. Manning was calm about the balance. “We finished several drives the way we wanted,” he said. “The throws that gave them the ball still belong to me. The next opponent gets the whole game to look at, so we have to look at all of it as well.”
A second return, then another interception

body.alt: Editorial illustration of Jolt Train Ln (Jolteon), number 9, NeMarcus Tare (Ninetales), number 42.
body.caption: Jolt Train Ln scored twice on returns, while NeMarcus Tare recorded three sacks.

body.text: Viridian forced Saffron's only punt shortly after its fourth-quarter field goal. That could have supplied a modest foothold for the Titans, but their next series moved backward and ended with another Octillery punt. Jolt Train Ln caught this one at the Saffron twenty-three and returned it seventy-seven yards for his second touchdown.

The returner's final line was four returns for 185 yards and two touchdowns. That is enough work for a featured performance before the defensive contribution is counted. With 1:12 remaining, he intercepted Mr. Rime and returned the ball ten yards. Manning threw a thirty-one-yard touchdown pass to Lamb on the next play, completing Saffron's scoring.

Lamb finished with six catches for 131 yards and two touchdowns. Witten, Skattebo and Woobat supplied the other receiving scores. Manning completed fifteen of twenty-four passes for 218 yards and was not sacked. Pickens caught all three of his targets for forty-two yards. The passing production spread across different types of possessions, from the long first-half march to the one-play finish after the late interception.

NeMarcus Tare helped make those extra possessions possible. He received credit for three sacks, twelve pressures and a forced fumble. Ampharos had seven tackles and the interception that set up Witten's touchdown. Furfrou recorded eight tackles and a forced fumble, while Honedge recovered Dewott's fourth-quarter fumble. Saffron conceded yards at times, especially to Dragonair, whose eight catches produced 125, but repeatedly prevented those gains from becoming touchdowns.
Mt. Silver is next

Viridian drops to 4–9 and visits Violet in Week 15. Gabite's eighty rushing yards and Dragonair's receiving production show that the Titans found individual successes. Those successes came with two interceptions, one lost fumble and two catastrophic punt returns allowed. A complete recovery requires attention to the possessions ending with the kicking team as well as the ones involving Mr. Rime.

Saffron travels with a healthier immediate availability picture: no player in its current injury report has a positive remaining absence. That does not remove the difficulty of facing Mt. Silver, which has allowed 105 points in thirteen games and just beat Mahogany 23–7. Saffron has allowed seventy-nine. Both teams have substantial reasons to believe their defense can control an important afternoon.

Scarboro welcomed the prospect. “This is the kind of game you work to earn,” he said. “I believe in these players. I believe in the preparation. And if something needs to be better, it starts with me getting it right with them.” His team supplied fifty-six points against Viridian; the next test will ask how many of those finishing opportunities it can create against a fellow conference contender.

art.alt: Editorial illustration of Jolt Train Ln (Jolteon), number 9.

articles.title: Lavender makes thirteen points stand up
articles.dek: A second-quarter touchdown, two kicks from Just a cactus and a defense that allowed one third-down conversion carry the Wails past Azalea, 13–3.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Travis Scarboro was asked whether a 13–3 victory over Azalea demonstrated Lavender's growing confidence. “It demonstrates thirteen points and three points,” he said. Asked about the defense's work on third down, the Wails coach became considerably more expansive. He discussed the value of forcing another snap, the difference between a useful short completion and a conversion, and the need to finish the possession after playing two good downs. The first question had been too large. The second had given him something to work with.

Lavender held Azalea to one conversion in ten third-down attempts, intercepted a threatening second-quarter drive and allowed no touchdown. Those were the essentials of a win that moved the Wails to 8–5. Their offense supplied one touchdown and two field goals. It was sufficient against a Swarm team that punted six times and managed only a late-third-quarter field goal.

The result keeps Lavender in a useful position in the Kanto–Johto playoff race, with Celadon visiting next. The Wails remain behind Blackthorn in Johto East, but their eighth victory gives them another week of pursuing a postseason place from inside the current field. Azalea drops to 5–8 and now faces a Cerulean side that has just beaten Cinnabar by one point. The Swarm will need more from their possessions than they found here.

This game offered few easy yards. The teams combined for eleven punts. Frosmoth completed eighteen of thirty-four passes for 162 yards and a touchdown; Azalea's Drampa completed eighteen of thirty-one for 144 yards and an interception. Lavender held a modest 222–196 advantage in total yards. The margin came from the way a handful of possessions ended, which is exactly the part Scarboro preferred to discuss.
The nine-play drive that supplied the touchdown

body.alt: Editorial illustration of Frosmoth (Frosmoth), number 15, Beedrill (Beedrill), number 93.
body.caption: Frosmoth found Beedrill for a four-yard touchdown.

body.text: The first five possessions ended in punts. Neither offense had established enough continuity to make a score feel imminent. Then Lavender put together a nine-play, seventy-one-yard drive beginning at 4:47 of the second quarter, with five different players carrying the ball or completing receptions by the time Beedrill caught the touchdown.

Frosmoth opened with a two-yard completion to the rushing Mauler Twin, number ninety-five, then found Luvdisc for eight yards through the middle. Mauler Twin ran for thirteen up the middle, and Might Guy followed with a twenty-three-yard reception deep right. The Wails had crossed significant ground without asking one player to manufacture everything.

Two incomplete throws to Unfezant interrupted that progress. On third-and-ten, Frosmoth went short left to Wailord for twelve yards. That completion kept the possession alive and deserves a place beside the eventual score. A drive can include a long reception and still end empty if the next third down goes wrong; Wailord gave Lavender another set of opportunities.

Beedrill then caught an eight-yard pass short right and returned to the same broad area for a four-yard touchdown at 2:38. The receiver finished with only two catches for twelve yards, both on that scoring series. A small receiving total can describe a very useful afternoon when it contains the catch that puts the team ahead and the one that creates it.

“I was glad he came back to me,” Beedrill said. “Everybody had already helped us get there. I wanted to finish that part for them.” The gentle explanation suited an offensive possession in which several players had done their share before the final two throws. Frosmoth, less inclined to linger, supplied a brisker account: “We got moving, had to fix third down, and finished. We need more drives like that.”

Just a cactus added the extra point. Lavender had the first seven points of the game and would keep the lead throughout. The next Azalea possession, however, made the difference between a lead and a comfortable afternoon very clear.
Nidorina preserves the lead

body.alt: Editorial illustration of Doc Ock (Octillery), number 97.
body.caption: Doc Ock recorded five tackles as Lavender held Blackthorn to three points.

body.text: Azalea answered with its most substantial drive of the half. Drampa connected with Hippopotas, Ursaring and Kricketune as the Swarm covered fifty-three yards. A twenty-yard pass deep right to Kricketune gave the visitors a particularly useful gain, and a later seven-yard completion to Machop brought up third-and-three.

At fifty-two seconds remaining, Drampa threw short left. Nidorina intercepted the pass and returned it twenty-one yards, ending a nine-play possession without points. Lavender's offense did not turn the takeaway into another score, but the defensive value was already considerable. Azalea had finally moved with purpose and still entered halftime trailing 7–0.

“They were putting completions together,” Nidorina said. “That means you have to finish your own play. I wanted the ball, and once I had it I wanted more yards.” The defender's directness reflected the consequence of the interception. The Swarm's best first-half opportunity had required time and several successful snaps. One successful defensive play ended all of it.

Lavender's pass rush contributed at separate stages. Gumshoos sacked Drampa for five yards on a third-and-one early in the second quarter. The defensive Mauler Twin, number ninety-two, recorded a sack, three tackles for loss and six pressures. Axew eventually supplied the final fourth-down sack. Keeping the two Mauler Twins straight is worthwhile: number ninety-five carried ten times for fifty-five yards; number ninety-two made the quarterback's afternoon less pleasant.

Scarboro was willing to explain that distinction, too. “Different jobs,” he said. “Both have to do them. If you're asking about the rush, ask about the rush. If you're asking about the run, ask about the run.” It was a reasonably complete answer by his standards, particularly for anyone who had begun the interview hoping for a broad statement about momentum.
Two field goals preserve the separation

Lavender opened the second half with a ten-play, forty-five-yard possession. Just a cactus finished it with a thirty-nine-yard field goal at 4:02 of the third quarter, extending the lead to 10–0. Azalea later matched that kick's distance: Sunflora converted from thirty-nine yards with three seconds left in the period, bringing the Swarm within a touchdown.

The Wails responded with the sort of possession that does important work without producing a dazzling finish. Beginning at 5:58 of the fourth, they held the ball through thirteen plays and moved sixty-six yards. Wailord caught passes for six and fourteen. Unfezant supplied seven. Mauler Twin ran right for ten, Luvdisc caught eight, and Machoke added two useful rushing gains.

Samurott's eleven-yard reception advanced the drive again before three incomplete passes forced the field-goal decision. Just a cactus made the thirty-two-yard kick at 3:03. Lavender had consumed nearly three minutes and restored a ten-point advantage. Azalea now needed two scoring possessions from an offense that had produced one field goal all game.

Luvdisc led Lavender with six catches for forty-four yards, while Unfezant had forty-one yards on three receptions. Wailord caught four passes for twenty-nine. Those modest totals fit a game built from short advances rather than repeated explosive plays. They also show why the thirteen-play fourth-quarter drive mattered: the Wails had to keep doing the routine work successfully for a sustained stretch.

“I just try to give him a place to put the ball,” Luvdisc said. “Some of the catches aren't very long. If they let us take another snap in a better place, that's useful.” The receiver's modest account was a fair summary of an offense that needed each conversion to protect its narrow supply of points.
Axew supplies the last stop

Azalea punted after the field goal, forced Lavender to punt in return and regained possession with 1:05 remaining. Drampa found Pyroar for twelve yards, but the drive stalled. On fourth-and-six with thirty-four seconds left, Axew sacked him for seven yards. Frosmoth needed one kneel to finish the game.

The Wails enter the Celadon matchup with People Eater still listed out three weeks and Hobbes out one. Dugtrio has a new one-week absence after this game. Those limitations give the remaining players meaningful responsibilities, particularly when an offense is operating with little spare scoring. The current record establishes the absences; it does not promise an immediate return to a particular role when a counter reaches zero.

Azalea's Ursaring gained fifty-three yards on thirteen carries, but no receiver exceeded twenty-eight yards. The Swarm's defense allowed only one touchdown and kept several Lavender possessions brief. Its work deserved more help. Scarboro could leave the final word to the numbers he had preferred at the beginning: thirteen points scored, three allowed, and another opponent stopped on fourth down.

art.alt: Editorial illustration of Just a cactus (Maractus), number 12.

articles.title: Gyarzalez catches everything while Mt. Silver works through the errors
articles.dek: Tony Gyarzalez went eight-for-eight on his targets, Gregar Jenings gained 160 yards, and the Reds beat Mahogany 23–7 before Saffron comes to town.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Tony Gyarzalez received eight targets at Mahogany and caught all eight. Mt. Silver could have used that degree of certainty earlier in the afternoon, when its first three possessions produced two interceptions and a punt. The Reds eventually won 23–7, reached 12–1 and gave Connor McLarren enough good material to make a joke without pretending the entire performance had been tidy.

“We kept giving them invitations in the first quarter,” McLarren said. “Very hospitable of us. Fortunately, the defense wasn't interested in hosting a party.” He had a more direct assessment of Gyarzalez: “Eight throws, eight catches. We ought to see if he can explain that arrangement to everybody.”

Gyarzalez finished with 106 receiving yards and a touchdown. Gregar Jenings added seven catches for 160 yards and another score, giving Tic Thorpe two dependable destinations once the passing offense recovered from its early mistakes. Thorpe completed twenty-four of thirty-seven throws for 335 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions. Mt. Silver gained 386 total yards to Mahogany's 202.

The defense made the uneven opening survivable. Mahogany punted eight times, converted two of thirteen third downs and did not score until 1:24 remained in the fourth quarter. The Frost got opportunities from their own defense, particularly Lopunny and Bruxish, but could not convert those opportunities into an early lead. A scoreless first quarter gradually became a game in which the Reds had room to work through their problems.

The stakes rise immediately. Saffron arrives next at 11–2 after beating Viridian 56–6. Mt. Silver retains its place at the top of the current Kanto–Johto seeds, with Blackthorn and Saffron close enough to make the next result consequential. All three have four regular-season games remaining. McLarren will have an audience for any additional remarks about generosity. He would prefer his offense to stop providing the examples.
Two interceptions, no early damage

Lopunny intercepted Thorpe's first pass, a deep throw right at 5:26 of the opening quarter, and returned it fourteen yards. Mahogany's ensuing possession gained three yards and ended with a punt. The Frost had prevented the Reds from building anything and then failed to build much of their own.

Bruxish sacked Thorpe on Mt. Silver's next possession, helping force another punt. Later in the quarter, Bruxish recorded a second sack, leaving third-and-seventeen. Thorpe again threw deep right, and Lopunny again intercepted him, this time returning the ball twenty-two yards. Two interceptions by the same defender on the same broad side of the field were a clear problem for the visiting passing game.

Mahogany's response ended on downs after four plays and eight yards. The Frost could claim an excellent opening quarter defensively, yet had no points to show for it. That was an expensive outcome against an opponent capable of recovering through its receivers. The longer the game stayed scoreless, the longer Mt. Silver had to find a workable sequence.

Thorpe did not try to turn the start into a grand statement about resilience. “I made two throws that gave them the ball,” he said. “The defense got us another chance. I needed to use it better.” His quiet account was more useful than a celebration of the eventual yardage. The mistakes were real, and so was the protection provided by the other unit.

Mahogany's defense kept making individual plays. Bruxish finished with three sacks and six pressures, while Lopunny added three passes defended to the two interceptions. Those performances deserve recognition even though the Frost lost. They created the conditions for a competitive afternoon. Their offense repeatedly gave those conditions back through short possessions.
Thorpe finds two reliable targets

body.alt: Gengar Gregar Jenings in Mt. Silver's crimson number88 carrying the ball near the end zone.
body.caption: Gregar Jenings scored on a thirty-yard reception and finished with 160 receiving yards.

body.text: Mt. Silver finally scored on a four-play, eighty-six-yard possession late in the second quarter. Vibrava opened with a five-yard run left. Thorpe then found Jenings deep right for sixty yards and Gyarzalez through the middle for twenty-one. Raticate completed the drive with a one-yard touchdown run at the two-minute mark.

The touchdown demonstrated how rapidly the Reds could change the game once they completed the long throw. Jenings' sixty-yard reception did most of the work in one snap, but Gyarzalez made the next one productive enough to leave the offense at the goal line. Mahogany had spent a long time keeping Mt. Silver scoreless; the decisive march lasted fifty-three seconds.

The Reds followed with a ten-play, eighty-yard possession before halftime. Scep Smith Jr. converted third-and-ten with an eleven-yard reception. Gyarzalez caught a twenty-five-yard pass deep left, Vulpix added sixteen deep right, and Raticate supplied an eleven-yard run. Adam Venutieri finished with an eighteen-yard field goal at eleven seconds remaining. Mt. Silver led 10–0 despite its earlier turnovers.

Gyarzalez described the work without embellishment. “If he comes back to me, I want the result to be dependable,” he said. “A short completion can be the one that lets us keep going. The next throw might be the big one.” Eight catches on eight targets supported the description. The receiver gave Thorpe productive options at several distances, including the touchdown that would extend the lead in the fourth quarter.

Jenings took the larger gains. On the first drive after halftime, he caught passes for ten and twenty-five yards before finishing with a thirty-yard touchdown deep left at 4:19. The six-play possession covered seventy-six yards. Mt. Silver had followed the first-half recovery with another sustained scoring drive, stretching the lead to seventeen.
The giveaways still require work

body.alt: Overhead illustration of Togekiss Tic Thorpe in crimson number42 preparing to pass.
body.caption: Tic Thorpe threw for 335 yards as Mt. Silver worked through an uneven start.

body.text: The next two possessions traded fumbles. Exploud lost the ball on a run left, with Porygon-Z recovering for Mt. Silver. Three plays later, Scep Smith Jr. fumbled after a short completion and Mahogany recovered. The Reds had gained a promising extra possession and surrendered it almost immediately.

McLarren allowed himself a dry assessment. “We were apparently worried they hadn't had enough chances,” he said. “I'd like to be a little less considerate next week.” The humor had an obvious football basis. Mt. Silver finished with three turnovers. Saffron's ability to score through offense, defense and returns makes that kind of generosity particularly dangerous in the upcoming matchup.

The Reds also managed only fifty-one rushing yards. Vibrava led with thirty-two on seven attempts, while Raticate gained twenty-one on four and scored the team's rushing touchdown. The passing game carried most of the offense. That arrangement worked against Mahogany, especially once Jenings and Gyarzalez began stacking completions, but the running contribution remains part of the preparation for a stronger opponent.

The final touchdown drive began near the end of the third quarter. Gyarzalez converted third-and-ten with an eleven-yard catch, Jenings added twenty-one, and Raticate caught a fourteen-yard pass on the first snap of the fourth. Three productive runs followed before Thorpe found Gyarzalez short right for ten yards and a touchdown at 4:42. The Reds had covered seventy-four yards in nine plays.
The late answer lasts one possession

Mahogany eventually scored on an eleven-play, seventy-yard drive. Porygon-Z converted fourth-and-fourteen with a fourteen-yard throw to Wobbuffet, then hit Skiploom short right for a six-yard touchdown. The Frost recovered the ensuing onside kick and briefly had another chance to change the final minutes.

Blayz Matthews sacked Porygon-Z on the first snap after the recovery. Mahogany could not repair the lost yardage, and a fourth-and-fourteen completion to Bibarel gained only eight. Thorpe knelt twice to finish the game. Matthews received credit for two sacks and five pressures, with the late sack providing a clear answer to Mahogany's last burst of momentum.

The Frost fall to 3–9–1 and host Pewter next. Exploud's seventeen carries produced forty-seven yards, and Porygon-Z finished with 137 passing yards. Better early possessions would have given their defense something tangible for its work. Mt. Silver, meanwhile, has a week to prepare for Saffron with Josh Alakazam still unavailable and Thorpe carrying the passing responsibility. Gyarzalez supplied eight catches without a miss; the Reds will want more of that precision when the Psi Corps arrive.

articles.title: Gibby Timmy needs eight seconds to take the lead back
articles.dek: Rustboro survives two lost fumbles, answers Fortree’s late field goal with a 59-yard touchdown and closes a 29–23 road win on fourth down.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Fortree spent thirteen plays reclaiming the lead. Rustboro answered in one. Shawn Watzon threw deep left to Gibby Timmy for a fifty-nine-yard touchdown at 3:34 of the fourth quarter, turning a 23–21 deficit into the lead the Stone would carry to a 29–23 victory. The touchdown possession consumed eight seconds. Fortree's preceding field-goal drive had consumed more than three minutes.

Tyler Scarboro considered the difference with the interest of someone examining two very different routes to the same destination. “People will take the scenic road and tell you all about the trees,” Rustboro's coach said. “Sometimes the road goes straight where you need it to go. We had a receiver going that direction, and Shawn got him the ball. I don't think we need to complicate that part.”

There was ample complication elsewhere. Rustboro fell behind 14–0 before its offense took its first snap, lost two fumbles and failed to finish a long second-quarter drive. The Stone still produced 409 yards, punted once and improved to 8–5. Watzon completed sixteen of twenty-four passes for 276 yards and two touchdowns, both to Gibby Timmy, without an interception.

Gibby Timmy caught three passes for 138 yards. Two of them were the fifty-two- and fifty-nine-yard touchdowns that supplied Rustboro's most immediate answers to trouble. The other was a twenty-eight-yard reception on fourth-and-one during a long third-quarter scoring drive. Three catches covered a remarkable range of responsibilities: start the comeback, keep a possession alive and take back the game.

The victory leaves Rustboro within a game of Petalburg in Hoenn West and fifth in the current Hoenn–Sinnoh seeds. A visit to 10–3 Sunyshore comes next. Fortree, now 3–10, heads to Oreburgh after another loss that included enough encouraging moments to make the eventual result especially frustrating.
Two long throws undo the early damage

body.alt: Porygon-Z Shawn Watzon number37 throwing toward Archeops Gibby Timmy number99 in Rustboro brown and silver.
body.caption: Shawn Watzon and Gibby Timmy connected for two long touchdowns at Fortree.

body.text: Fortree opened with an eighty-yard touchdown drive, finished by Palpitoad's seven-yard run up the middle. The Skyhawks then recovered Gibby Timmy's fumble on the ensuing kickoff return at the Rustboro twenty-four. Four plays later, Floatzel scored from a yard out, and the home team led 14–0.

Rustboro's offense had yet to touch the ball. That detail makes the beginning more awkward for the returner, whose later receiving production would become the central story of the win. The Stone did not have to choose between acknowledging the mistake and using one of their most dangerous players. Watzon went back to him on their first offensive possession.

At 2:24 of the first quarter, Watzon found Gibby Timmy deep left for fifty-two yards and a touchdown. The five-play drive covered eighty yards. Rustboro had recovered one score promptly enough to keep the opening sequence from defining the entire game.

“I owed us something useful after the return,” Gibby Timmy said. “I figured getting all the way to their end zone might improve the conversation.” The receiver's grin was easy to hear in the answer, but the repayment was tangible. His next two catches would also come at moments when the Stone needed a substantial result.

Rustboro's next touchdown required more ordinary work. SEARED BITE caught a twenty-eight-yard pass short left to begin the possession, Shieldon added five, and Philly ran for six. Watchog converted a third-and-one with a seven-yard run. The drive crossed into the second quarter before Watzon scored on a three-yard run up the middle, tying the game at fourteen.

Fortree responded immediately through another eighty-yard drive, ending with Palpitoad's second touchdown run, this one from a yard out. The unsuccessful extra point left the Skyhawks ahead 20–14. Their early offense had produced three rushing touchdowns from relatively short finishing distances, while the passing game supplied territory between them. Rabsca would finish with 230 passing yards, including seventy-four receiving yards for Floatzel and fifty-six for Haunter.
A long drive with no reward

Rustboro then spent thirteen plays moving sixty-eight yards without scoring. Watzon's running helped sustain the possession, Watchog gained thirteen and seven on consecutive carries, and Lombre caught passes for twelve and fifteen. Those gains brought the Stone close enough to threaten the lead before the drive stalled.

Loudred sacked Watzon on third-and-four for a four-yard loss. On fourth down, Kingdra broke up the short throw intended for SEARED BITE. Rustboro had used more than three minutes and still trailed by six. Scarboro had a simple diagnosis of that sequence: “Getting close is useful only if you do something when you get there. We did a lot of traveling and came home without the thing we went to get.”

The first offensive possession after halftime ended with another lost fumble, this time by Philly on a short run. Fortree took over with a chance to extend its lead, but Rustboro's defense forced a punt after a drive that lost seven yards. The defensive answer kept the margin at six and gave the offense another opportunity to make its longer possessions worthwhile.

Rustboro took that opportunity through an eighty-yard, thirteen-play touchdown drive. Philly gained eleven up the middle, SEARED BITE caught nine, and Watzon converted fourth-and-one with the twenty-eight-yard throw deep right to Gibby Timmy. The choice produced considerably more than the minimum distance required and prevented another promising drive from ending empty.

The Stone continued through short passes, quarterback runs and contributions from Watchog. Philly finished from a yard out to the right at 1:07 of the third quarter. The extra point gave Rustboro its first lead, 21–20. The drive lasted three minutes and forty seconds, a useful contrast with the explosive touchdown still to come.

Philly finished with fifty-two rushing yards and a touchdown on eleven carries. Watchog added forty on seven attempts, and Watzon supplied thirty-eight rushing yards and a score. “We had enough room to finish that one,” Philly said. “After putting the ball down earlier, I wasn't interested in making another excuse.” The back would have another important job in the final minute.
Joe ends Fortree’s final chance

body.alt: Pink Luvdisc Joe wearing Rustboro's brown and silver number43 beside a football.
body.caption: Joe's fourth-quarter interception gave Rustboro possession for its closing drive.

body.text: Fortree responded to the third-quarter touchdown with its own long possession, covering fifty-eight yards before Lanturn made a thirty-six-yard field goal at 3:41 of the fourth. The Skyhawks led 23–21. Rustboro's next offensive snap became the fifty-nine-yard touchdown to Gibby Timmy, followed by Watzon's successful two-point pass to Philly.

The conversion established a six-point lead and forced Fortree to pursue a touchdown. The Skyhawks gained twenty-one yards on their next drive before facing fourth-and-one. Rabsca threw deep right at 2:11. Joe intercepted the pass and returned it nineteen yards, giving Rustboro possession with 2:04 remaining.

“Catch it first, get what you can, then let the offense work,” Joe said. “They still had to finish it.” The defender's practical account was correct. Rustboro had the ball and the lead, but the remaining time required more than an immediate kneel. The Stone needed another sequence of successful plays to keep Fortree from getting one last opportunity.

Watzon found SEARED BITE for fifteen yards and Shieldon for another fifteen. Philly ran right for six, and Watzon later ran left for four. On fourth-and-one with 1:07 remaining, Philly gained two yards up the middle. That conversion ended Fortree's realistic chance to regain possession. Watzon knelt with twenty-eight seconds left.
Sunyshore will test the same habits

Rustboro's offense combined explosive receiving with enough running to keep its drives moving. SEARED BITE caught four passes for sixty-two yards, while Shieldon and Lombre each had twenty-seven receiving yards. Watzon took only one sack and avoided an interception. The two lost fumbles and failed goal-line approach remain substantial corrections, especially before facing a defense that has just shut out Canalave.

Sunyshore's 17–0 victory included a defensive touchdown, four sacks and two interceptions. Rustboro will travel with My Way, Son still listed out four weeks. The Stone have already shown productive alternatives on the ground, but protecting possessions will matter as much as finding yardage. Scarboro can enjoy the direct route taken by the final touchdown while still insisting that the earlier detours be explained.

Fortree scored only three points after halftime. Its early rushing touchdowns and Rabsca's larger completions created a winnable game, but the final fourth-down interception ended the last chance to regain the lead. Rustboro's final fourth down had the opposite result: Philly carried through the middle for two yards, and the Stone kept the ball until the clock expired.

articles.title: Rothington supplies the touchdown Sunyshore had been waiting for
articles.dek: Ash Rothington’s 34-yard interception return breaks open a defensive afternoon as the Starseekers shut out Canalave, 17–0, and reach ten wins.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Ash Rothington intercepted Slowking's short pass right, returned it thirty-four yards and gave Sunyshore its first touchdown of the game. The Starseekers' offense had spent much of the afternoon trying to produce that result. Their defense finally supplied it directly, turning a 3–0 lead into a two-score advantage late in the third quarter of a 17–0 victory over Canalave.

Karson Jones was happy to give that unit the attention. “If you're coming to watch us, make sure you're watching everybody,” the Sunyshore coach said. “There are players on that defense who expect to decide a game. Ash didn't wait for somebody else to make it happen. That's the standard we want people to recognize when they see this team.”

Sunyshore improves to 10–3 and remains the Sinnoh East leader. Canalave falls to 7–6, still occupying the seventh position in the current Hoenn–Sinnoh seeds but facing the immediate prospect of hosting unbeaten Mossdeep. The Starseekers host Rustboro next. Both games will test whether the defensive work shown here can survive a substantially more productive opposing offense.

Canalave managed 116 total yards, including fifty-five passing yards from Slowking. Its thirty-three rushing attempts produced sixty-one yards. The Bulwark avoided losing a fumble and converted five of fourteen third downs, but rarely gained enough territory after those conversions to threaten a score. Sunyshore could afford an uneven offensive afternoon because its defense repeatedly prevented the next possession from becoming dangerous.

That permission had limits. DeZhaun Watzon threw two interceptions, and BAXXED? lost a late fumble. The Starseekers gained 221 yards and scored one offensive touchdown. Their defense deserved the lead role in this account, and Jones had reason to make sure the rest of his roster understood why.
A field goal is the first separation

The opening quarter produced no points. Canalave used nine plays on its first possession, gaining thirty-four yards before punting. Sunyshore's first drive ended when Froslass intercepted Watzon's deep throw right. The Starseekers answered defensively with a sack by Fred Whirler, and Canalave soon punted again.

Don Philliams supplied another sack early in the second quarter. Two plays later, on third-and-seventeen, 88 Special intercepted Slowking's deep pass left and returned it sixteen yards. Sunyshore had created the chance that eventually produced its first points, though completing that scoring possession required more work than simply accepting the turnover.

Fera LaGatr converted third-and-five with a thirteen-yard catch short left. Jolt Vick then caught a thirty-two-yard pass deep left, the longest completion of Sunyshore's game. EKTRIK RED added four yards, but Absol sacked Watzon near the end of the drive, and an incomplete third-down pass forced the Starseekers to settle for a kick.

Duo SON 😭 made the twenty-six-yard field goal at 2:49 of the second quarter. Sunyshore led 3–0 and would carry that advantage into halftime. Neither offense scored again before the break. The Starseekers' final two first-half possessions ended in punts, while Canalave also continued giving the ball back.

Jones distinguished belief in the offense from satisfaction with the result. “I expect our players to handle being expected to win,” he said. “That includes when the first half doesn't look the way you wanted. You don't get to act surprised that somebody is making it difficult. You get back out there and do the work.” The defense had already done enough work to ensure the offense had time.
Rothington changes the score himself

body.alt: Donphan Don Philliams number44 and Poliwrath Fred Whirler number56 in Sunyshore pink and black.
body.caption: Don Philliams and Fred Whirler combined for three credited sacks in Sunyshore's shutout.

body.text: Sunyshore opened the second half with a sixty-six-yard drive. FLOAT SZN began with runs of nine and eight yards. Jolt Vick converted third-and-eight with a ten-yard catch, and Scol Alexander later caught a twenty-eight-yard pass deep right. The Starseekers had assembled the sort of possession that could have given the defense a comfortable margin.

Instead, Weezing intercepted Watzon's short throw left at 3:36 of the third quarter and returned it eighteen yards. The drive had consumed nine plays and more than two minutes without adding a point. Canalave had another chance to turn a defensive takeaway into a meaningful response.

The Bulwark moved through several short runs, with Doduo carrying repeatedly and Slowking converting a third-and-one himself. The gains were modest enough that Canalave soon faced third-and-seven. Slowking went short right. Rothington took the pass and returned it for the touchdown at 1:55, giving Sunyshore a result its offense had been unable to secure.

Rothington's account was measured. “Once I had it, I wanted to make the possession count,” he said. “We'd been keeping them out. Getting points ourselves helped the whole team.” His final defensive line included five tackles, a tackle for loss, a pass defended and the interception touchdown. The calm delivery did little to diminish the importance of the play.

The score was also a reward for the work that preceded it. Canalave's short runs had kept the series alive without creating a large gain. Sunyshore still had the opportunity to defend an obvious passing situation, and Rothington finished it. The two defensive interceptions came on third-and-seventeen and third-and-seven, both after the Bulwark had struggled to improve its position.
One offensive touchdown supplies the cushion

body.alt: Scolipede Scol Alexander wearing Sunyshore number58 with the ball near the goal line.
body.caption: Scol Alexander's four-yard touchdown catch gave Sunyshore a seventeen-point lead.

body.text: Canalave punted again after the interception return. Sunyshore began the fourth quarter with a forty-four-yard drive and finally completed an offensive touchdown possession. BAXXED? ran for three and eight yards, Fera LaGatr caught seven, and the back supplied another six on the ground.

Watzon then found Scol Alexander short right for fourteen yards. After another short run, he returned to the same receiver and broad side of the field for a four-yard touchdown at 4:03. The seven-play drive took nearly two minutes and made the lead seventeen points. For the first time, the offense had converted its progress into the full reward.

Scol Alexander finished with three receptions for forty-six yards and the touchdown. “The earlier catch gets you closer,” the receiver said. “You still have to complete the next one properly. I wanted the last few yards to be as clean as the first part of the drive.” The careful explanation fit a performance in which three catches supplied a long gain, a useful approach and the finish.

Fera LaGatr led Sunyshore with seven catches for forty-nine yards, providing regular short completions. Jolt Vick had forty-two yards on two catches. Watzon completed seventeen of twenty-eight passes for 163 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. Those figures describe a functional but inconsistent passing game, with the fourth-quarter scoring drive giving it a much better conclusion than the earlier giveaways suggested.

The running game produced fifty-eight yards. FLOAT SZN gained thirty on five carries, and BAXXED? had twenty-eight on eight. The latter lost a fumble with thirty-nine seconds remaining, giving Canalave one more possession. That mistake did not change the result, but it belongs in the review alongside the two intercepted throws.
A shutout with new absences

Whirler and Philliams each received credit for one and a half sacks. THE BRIZZLER supplied another, bringing Sunyshore's total to four. The final sack came on Canalave's last snap, when THE BRIZZLER reached Slowking for a seven-yard loss with ten seconds showing. The Bulwark had gained some late territory but again finished without points.

Canalave's defense had done useful work of its own. Weezing recorded seven tackles, an interception, a forced fumble and a recovery, while Froslass supplied the other interception. Those takeaways kept the game close for much of the afternoon. The offense's inability to capitalize meant the defense was repeatedly asked to protect a small deficit until Sunyshore finally expanded it.

The Starseekers leave with two new reported absences: Serp Gardener is out two weeks, and FLOAT SZN is out one. Their production and roles make those meaningful changes before Rustboro visits. The game record does not establish when either injury occurred, so the next week's preparation should begin with the confirmed availability rather than a guessed injury scene.

Jones kept his confidence while acknowledging the workload ahead. “Ten wins gives us ten wins,” he said. “People are going to expect the next one now. Our job is to prepare the players who are available and be ready for that attention.” Rothington's return supplied the decisive separation this time. Rustboro arrives having thrown for two long touchdowns at Fortree, which will give Sunyshore's defense a different kind of passing game to stop.
